opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this goes back to the work we did with Chris Lu and others on Discovered Policy Optimisation. The setup was that we used the mirror learning framework, which gives you a space of RL algorithms that all come with theoretical guarantees, things like monotonic improvement and convergence, as long as the drift function satisfies certain conditions. PPO turns out to be one point in that space. So instead of hand-designing the algorithm, we parameterised the drift function with a small neural network and meta-learned it with evolution strategies across environments.

The interesting part is what you do once you have that learned function. A neural network sitting inside your update rule is a black box. You can run it, but you don't really know why it works or whether it will generalise beyond the meta-training distribution. So we plotted it and looked at its shape: how it treats positive versus negative advantages, and how it penalises the policy for moving away from the old policy as the probability ratio changes. Then we asked whether we could write down a simple closed-form expression that captured the key qualitative features. That gave us DPO, which is a few lines of maths you can drop into a PPO implementation.

There are a few reasons that matters to me.

First, generalisation and robustness. Neural networks are notoriously bad at extrapolating outside the range they were trained on. A compact symbolic expression is much more likely to behave sensibly in regimes the meta-learner never saw. You're applying an Occam's razor prior on top of what evolution found.

Second, scientific understanding. If the whole pipeline ends with "here's a black box that's slightly better," we haven't learned much. When you look at the discovered function, you can actually see what it's doing differently from PPO's clipping, for instance an asymmetry in how it handles optimism versus pessimism. That's a hypothesis about what matters in policy optimisation, and other people can test it, critique it, and build on it.

Third, adoption and trust. Practitioners will happily change one line in their loss function. They're much less likely to ship a meta-learned network inside their optimiser that they have to load from a checkpoint and can't reason about.

More broadly, I see this as a nice template for how AI-driven discovery and humans can work together. The machine searches a huge space far more efficiently than we can by hand, and the human is good at distilling the result into something compact, interpretable and transferable. Increasingly I think even the distillation step can be partly automated, with things like symbolic regression or language models proposing candidate expressions. But the principle stays the same: discovery is most valuable when it produces understanding, not just a better number on a benchmark.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that a learned update rule, as it comes out of the meta-optimizer, is just a black box. It's a neural network that tells you how to change your parameters given the gradient, and you can show empirically that it works, but you don't actually know *what* it's doing. And that matters for a few reasons.

The first is trust and generalization. If I hand you a learned optimizer and say "this beats Adam on these tasks," you have no idea whether it will fall apart the moment you change the architecture, or train for ten times longer, or go to a different domain. Meta-learned things are notorious for overfitting to the meta-training distribution. But once you sit down, look at the learned function, and realize, "oh, this is essentially a specific nonlinear transform of the normalized gradient with this particular saturation behaviour," then you have something you can reason about. You can ask: does this make sense? Why would this be a good idea? And often the answer turns out to be quite sensible, which gives you some confidence it'll transfer.

The second is that symbolic expressions are just a much better medium for science. A neural network with a few thousand parameters is not something I can communicate to you on a whiteboard. A one-line formula is. You can put it in a paper, other people can implement it in three lines of code, they can analyze it, they can prove things about it. That's the whole point: we want these discoveries to actually enter the body of knowledge rather than be an artifact sitting on someone's hard drive.

And the third, which I find quite exciting philosophically, is that it changes the role of the human. We're not writing the learning algorithm anymore; the meta-learning process is doing the search. But we're also not just blindly deploying what comes out. The human sits in the loop as the interpreter, the one who looks at the discovered thing, extracts the principle, and often simplifies it. In our experience the symbolic version is frequently *better* than the raw learned one, because you've stripped out noise and overfitting in the process of understanding it. So interpretation isn't just a nice-to-have for explainability; it's genuinely part of the discovery pipeline.

I'd also say there's a practical reason, which is that machine learning as a field moves by people adopting things. No one is going to adopt an optimizer they can't understand. They will adopt a formula they can look at and go, "huh, that's a clever idea."

r002.rationale: The response says symbolic formulas are easier to communicate and implement, but it does not identify them as a way to port the algorithm beyond its original software environment.

astra-6.text:
Because discovering an algorithm that works and understanding why it works are two different things. If the result is just another neural network, you can evaluate it, but it’s difficult to see what principle it has discovered or when that principle might fail. Writing the drift function symbolically gives us something we can reason about: how does it change the update, and what behavior does that encourage?

The human interpretation is a way of turning the result of a search into scientific understanding. Ideally, you come away with a simple idea that you can analyze, communicate, and use to design other algorithms, rather than just an artifact that performs well.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we wanted to get scientific understanding out of the discovery, rather than just another black box that happens to perform well. If you discover a learning algorithm represented by a neural network, you can test it and show that it works, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what it’s doing or why it works.

Having a human interpret the drift function and write it down symbolically makes the underlying mechanism explicit. You can reason about the update, see which features matter, and formulate hypotheses about when it should succeed or fail. It also gives you something you can communicate and build on. The interesting outcome is that the automated search teaches us a principle that we can then understand, rather than simply handing us an opaque artifact.
